Healthy eating for older adults

Fruit and
vegetables every day

Affordable, nutritious and easy to eat.

Fruit and vegetables give us vitamins, minerals and fibre. Fibre helps keep our bowels regular. The familiar produce at your local market can do the job.

Presenter notes

0:00–0:40. Ask, “What fruit did you have yesterday?” Take one or two replies. “The ordinary fruit and veg we already know can give us fibre, vitamins and minerals. Today, let’s look at how much to eat, what’s worth buying and how to make it easier to chew.” Hold up a rice bowl before moving on.

Daily portions

What does one serving look like?

Use a familiar rice bowl, about 250–300 mL.

2+fruit servings
3+vegetable servings

Choose fruit more often than juice. A fruit serving can be peeled, cut or mashed to suit your chewing.

See how 2 + 3 can fit into a day
  • Morning1 medium orange1 fruit serving
  • Lunch and afterwards½ bowl cooked greens and ½ bowl cut fruit1 vegetable serving + 1 fruit serving
  • Dinner½ bowl cooked broccoli and ½ bowl cooked carrots2 vegetable servings
Presenter notes

0:40–1:40. Hold up the bowl and show where halfway sits. “A medium orange is one fruit serving. Half a bowl of cut fruit can also be one. Half a bowl of cooked vegetables is one vegetable serving.” Tap each example as you speak.

1:40–2:30. Ask, “If half a bowl is one, what does a whole bowl of cooked vegetables count as?” Let someone say two. “Choose fruit more often than juice. You can peel it, chop it or mash it.” Then ask what they would buy for tomorrow.

Shopping on a budget

Buy what you’ll finish

Compare the price of what you’ll actually eat.

  1. Check what’s in season

    Compare the market prices of cabbage, leafy greens and carrots.

  2. Check the freezer and the label

    Plain frozen vegetables let you cook a little at a time if you have a freezer. Look for canned vegetables with no added salt and canned fruit packed in juice.

  3. Plan how you’ll use it

    Buy what you can use or store safely. A large pack is worth it when you can finish it.

Example prices in HK dollars

Which pack costs less per portion eaten?

Small pack

HK$12 for 3

HK$4per portion eaten

Large pack

HK$18 for 6

HK$6per portion eaten

If you only use three, the small pack costs less per portion eaten.

Presenter notes

2:30–3:40. Ask, “Which is cheapest at your nearby market today?” Let the group name a vegetable. Point to the two example packs. “If I eat only three from the big pack, I’ve paid six dollars for each one I ate.” Switch to Use all 6 and pause for the group to spot when the bigger pack saves money. If someone has no freezer, talk about buying a smaller amount of fresh produce.

In the kitchen

Make it easier to chew

Ripe fruit, stewed apple and tender vegetables give you options.

  1. Cut

    Peel firm fruit if that helps. Cut it into small pieces.

  2. Cook gently

    Stew apple with a splash of water and no added sugar. Cook vegetables until tender.

  3. Check with a fork

    The side of a fork should press easily through a piece of carrot. Chop or mash it if that helps.

Use a light hand with salt and salty sauces. Soft cooking still leaves fibre in the fruit or vegetable.

If you have trouble swallowing, ask your care team which texture suits you.

Presenter notes

3:40–4:30. Point to Cut, Cook, Check in that order. “Think of a firm apple. Peel and cut it, stew it gently, then see if a fork presses through.” Point out a ripe banana or papaya as another soft choice.

4:30–5:00. Ask the group to say back one thing that would make tomorrow’s meal easier to chew. “We’ve looked at the shopping bag and the kitchen. Let’s try three choices together.”

Quick quiz · 1 of 3

Whole orange or orange juice?

Which one usually gives you more fibre?

Presenter notes

5:00–6:15. “Assuming you can chew the fruit comfortably, which usually gives you more fibre?” Pause for about five seconds. Invite people to call out or point before you reveal. “The orange has more of its fibre. Think about how quickly a glass of juice can disappear.”

Quick quiz · 2 of 3

Fresh or frozen vegetables?

Which can be a nutritious choice?

Presenter notes

6:15–7:30. Let the group vote, then reveal. “Fresh vegetables and plain frozen vegetables both count. Which would you pick if you were cooking for one?” Take an answer about price, freezer space or how much someone would use.

Quick quiz · 3 of 3

Raw or soft-cooked carrots?

Which is usually easier to chew?

Presenter notes

7:30–8:45. Ask which one takes less effort to chew. After the reveal, mime pressing a fork through a carrot. “If the fork goes through easily, the carrot has softened. It still has fibre.”

Before you go

Three things to remember

Choose fruit more often than juice

Cook until soft to make chewing easier

Pick the affordable option you’ll use

What would you try tomorrow?

Choose one thing from today’s talk.

Presenter notes

8:45–10:00. “What’s one thing you’ll try tomorrow?” Let two people answer. If needed, cue them with a rice bowl, a price tag or a fork. “Thank you. Fruit more often than juice, choose what you’ll finish and cook it as soft as you need.”
